name: Arabana-Wangkanguru
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Arabana-Wangkangurru follows the majority of Australian languages in having a strong stress accent on the first syllable of a word. There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, initial primary stress; secondary on 3rd/5th/7th with a morpheme-initial override in polymorphemic words) rests on the language's standard reference grammar (Hercus 1994, PL C-128, 324 pp.), which we hold in full; the deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim on printed p.47 (§2.12) from the page scan, with the secondary-stress and morphological rule on p.48. Only defect: the long sources[0] cite gives 'pp. 48-49' where the printed pages are 47-48 (the domain locator's '47' is right) — a cosmetic locator fix, not a reclassify. Glottolog offers nothing better; a web search found no instrumental stress study of Arabana, and the one recent phonological analysis touching metrics (Harvey et al. 2019, downloaded, open) confirms initial primary stress and trochaic left-aligned footing citing Hercus 1994:47. No works still to obtain are warranted.

sources.quote: Arabana-WangkangUrrU follows the majority of Australian languages in having a strong stress accent on the first syllable of a word. There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes' ); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable. [...] As described by Dixon ( 1 980a: 1 38) for other Australian languages, longer words have a secondary stress on the third, fifth and seventh syllable, the secondary accent being marked here by a grave accent [...] In long words consisting of several morphemes another rule supersedes this: each bound morpheme of two or three syllables has a secondary accent on its first syllable. [...] There are however two situations in which this whole system is ignored. One is in exclamations, vocatives, and imperatives that are shouted with distortion of the final syllables. These always have the main accent on the final syllable [...] The other exceptional circumstance is in song, where any syllable can be stressed, and particularly the final one
sources.note: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable; secondary on 3rd/5th/7th syllables in long monomorphemic words, which matches the catalog rule string exactly. Refinement: in polymorphemic words a morphological rule supersedes the odd-syllable count (each bound morpheme of 2-3 syllables carries a secondary accent on its first syllable, e.g. katha-rnda-nangka-lipama), so the catalog's alternating pattern is only the default for long simple words. Exceptions: shouted exclamations/vocatives/imperatives take main accent on the final syllable; song allows any syllable, esp. the final; compound nouns hav

sources.note: The work is a kinship-pronoun study. Its Arabana-Wangkangurru section gives only a table of ordinary vs special dual/plural pronoun forms and three example sentences; no statement about word stress, accent, tone, vowel length, syllable weight or any phonological topic appears anywhere in the paper. The only 'stress'/'accent' strings in the text are non-prosodic ('emphatically stressed by our informants', p. 52; station managers 'with a noticeable Scottish accent', p. 50). Catalog entry (fixed, trochaic rule from Hercus 1994) is neither confirmed nor contradicted by this work.

tone.quote: In Arabana, this three-way opposition is neutralized in various ways. The full distinction is only found in onsets immediately following the tonic vowel, which is the first vowel in a word: e.g. /ˈparu/ 'bony bream' vs /ˈpaɾu/ 'yellow ochre' vs /ˈpaɻu/ 'light'. In coda position (before a consonant), there is no distinction. In other post-tonic onset positions, not immediately following the tonic vowel, the continuant is distinguished, but there is no tap vs trill distinction.
tone.locator: p. 1278, section 1 Introduction (also Abstract: 'The triple contrast only appears following the tonic vowel, which is the first vowel')
tone.summary: No tone described; word prominence: tonic (primary-stressed) vowel = first vowel of the word, which licenses the full rhotic contrast in the following onset.
